Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters: A Causal Intervention for Routing Collapse in Time Series Foundation Models
Download PDF
Hung Phan, Thuy T. Nguyen, Minh Ngoc Dinh, Nhat-Quang Tran 
03 May 2026 (modified: 28 May 2026)
NeurIPS 2026 Conference Submission
Conference, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, Reviewers, Authors
Revisions
CC BY 4.0
TL;DR: MoE adapters on instance-normalized time series foundation models collapse; eight causal controls isolate RevIN as the cause and prescribe raw-input routing (RR-MoA/SR-MoA/Residual-IA+), beating prior adapters and full fine-tuning.
Abstract:
Time series foundation models (TSFMs) commonly adapt to new data by attaching a single trainable head to a frozen backbone, a one-size-fits-all setup that underfits heterogeneous regimes. Replacing the head with a mixture of experts is the standard upgrade, but on instance-normalized backbones (the dominant TSFM design class) it fails: routing entropy collapses to zero and one expert absorbs every input, a failure we call normalization-induced routing collapse. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms do not repair it, because the cause is in the router's input, not its optimization. Pre-encoder normalization strips the statistics a router would need to tell regimes apart. A mutual-information decomposition makes this precise and yields a signal-ratio that, computed before training, predicts dataset vulnerability (Spearman 
). Eight causal controls, including a vision-modality replication, isolate instance normalization as the cause. The prescription is a minimal causal intervention: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA), which routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. Under a strictly frozen backbone, RR-MoA wins 54/54 comparisons against the strongest fixed adapter and significantly outperforms LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine-tuning. The effect generalizes across six backbones and an imputation task. Frozen RR-MoA also beats full fine-tuning by 12–79% (the Frozen Paradox); two architecturally distinct variants confirm the principle generalizes beyond this specific router. Code is provided in the supplementary material.

Official Review of Submission16168 by Reviewer Pm4m
Official Reviewby Reviewer Pm4m26 Jun 2026, 17:14 (modified: 23 Jul 2026, 21:58)Program Chairs, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, Reviewers Submitted, Authors, Reviewer Pm4mRevisions
Summary:
This paper studies why mixture of experts adapter heads can fail when adapting frozen time series foundation models. The authors identify normalization induced routing collapse, where a hidden state router collapses to a single expert within a few optimization steps when used with backbones that apply learnable affine instance normalization, such as RevIN in MOMENT. The paper argues that this failure is caused mainly by the router input rather than by the routing optimization itself, since RevIN removes per window mean and scale information that is important for distinguishing temporal regimes. This diagnosis is supported by a mutual information analysis, a training free signal ratio that correlates with collapse risk, and several causal controls, including normalization ablations, comparisons across backbones, and a replication in vision models. As a remedy, the authors propose RR-MoA, which routes using the raw input before normalization while keeping expert adaptation on frozen hidden states. The method is reported to outperform fixed adapters, LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine tuning across all evaluated settings, with additional variants used to support generality across multiple backbones, forecasting horizons, and an imputation task.

Contribution Type: General: Most submissions will fall into this type.
Strengths And Weaknesses:
Strengths

S1 — The paper studies an interesting problem setting that is practically important.

S2 — The paper is logically structured, making its contributions easy to follow.

S3 — The authors conducted extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.

Weaknesses

W1 — The abstract's "54/54 wins" and "beats full fine-tuning by 12–79%" are all measured against frozen-adapter / PEFT baselines, i.e., methods constrained to the same frozen-backbone regime the paper studies. Table 4, Appendix M, and Appendix P.3 show that the whole RR-MoA family is beaten in absolute MSE by a 49K-parameter DLinear (e.g., 0.680 vs 0.416 on ETTh1) and that the TSFM backbone is explicitly "dead weight" on several datasets. This is a material caveat that does not appear in the abstract or introduction. I would ask the authors to move the DLinear comparison and the backbone-contribution analysis into the main text and to reframe the contribution accordingly; as currently presented, the framing oversells a method whose absolute forecasting quality is below a trivial linear baseline.

W2 — Figure 2 is too simple and small; parts of it overlap, making it difficult to see clearly, and it fails to clearly illustrate the paper’s core modules and contributions.

W3 — The collapse mechanism predicts that backbones without learnable-affine encoder normalization should not collapse, and the paper confirms Moirai does not. Yet RR-MoA still "wins" 12–29% on Moirai. If there is no collapse to fix, this gain must come from something other than collapse-repair — most plausibly the predictive value of the raw signal itself, consistent with the Pure Raw-MLP result in P.3. This weakens the causal chain "collapse → raw routing is the fix," and the cross-backbone wins should not be presented as uniform validation of the diagnosis.

W4 — Closing the DLinear gap requires a 546-run sweep plus a stack of dataset-specific engineering choices (shared NLinear branch, b=−2 gate init, 5-epoch warmup, validation-based early stopping), after which the result is still only 5/6 match-or-beat at a −2.8% mean gap (ETTh1 still loses). Appendix P.3 then shows a backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE matches or beats the dual-stream variant on average, indicating the gains come largely from the raw/NLinear branch (essentially DLinear) rather than the TSFM. This makes Residual-IA+ read as heavy tuning to approach a linear baseline, and its generalization beyond these six benchmarks is unclear.

W5 — The (M,Σ)-centric account is in tension with the authors' own ablations. The sufficient-statistic router using only [μ,σ] degrades MSE by +48% (Appendix F), showing (μ,σ) is not sufficient, while temporal shuffling barely changes performance, indicating the router relies on order-invariant distributional content broader than (M,Σ). Since both Observation 1 and R(D) are built specifically around (M,Σ), the theory does not cleanly match the empirically operative signal.

W6 — Minor Issue:

Inconsistencies in router parameter counts: The main text, Fig. 2, and Table A.1 all list 853, while item 4 of the Checklist states ~1100.
An extra parenthesis is present in R(D) on line 146.
The statement “13–42% over RR-MoA on six datasets” on line 64 is incorrect, it should be over baselines.
The terms “finetuning” and “fine-tuning” are used inconsistently; they should be standardized to a single form.
Quality: 2: not good
Clarity: 2: not good
Significance: 3: good
Originality: 3: good
Questions:
The experiments use almost only 512 as input length and 96 as the forecasting horizon. If the input length and forecasting length change, do the methods and conclusion in the paper still hold?

α is not initialized inconsistently. Appendix K states that ℓ is initialized to 0, so α = σ(0) = 0.5, but afterward it says, “Initialize with 0.492 and decrease monotonically.” Where does this inconsistency come from?

If the author can address my concerns, I would raise my score.

Summary:
Problem Statement - Time series foundation models (TSFMs) like MOMENT, PatchTST, and TimesFM use instance normalization (RevIN) to handle distribution shift, subtracting per-window mean (
) and dividing by standard deviation (
) before encoding. When practitioners attach Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adapter heads to these frozen backbones, the router collapses to selecting a single expert—routing entropy drops to 0.000±0.000. This occurs because RevIN strips the per-window statistics (
, 
) that distinguish input regimes, leaving the router with homogenized hidden states that cannot differentiate between a calm baseline and a volatile spike.

Method - The proposed method applies a minimal causal intervention: route on raw pre-normalization input X_raw while experts consume the frozen backbone's hidden states H. The router is a lightweight Conv1d gate (853 parameters) that selects Top-2 of K=5 architecturally diverse experts (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d). This preserves the temporal statistics RevIN discards.

Experimental Setup -

6 LTSF benchmarks (ETTh1/h2, ETTm1/m2, Weather, Electricity)
6 TSFMs spanning 3 normalization regimes (MOMENT-small/large, Moirai, Moirai-MoE, Chronos, Timer-XL)
Forecasting (H∈{96,192,336,720}) and 20%-masked imputation
Fixed adapters, LoRA (108-run sweep), TRACE, AdaMix, independent ensembles, full fine-tuning, DLinear
Key Findings

RR-MoA wins 54/54 comparisons against best fixed adapters (26–79% MSE improvement)
Frozen RR-MoA beats full fine-tuning by 12–79% ("Frozen Paradox")
Signal ratio R(D) predicts raw-routing benefit at Spearman correlation

The evaluation focuses on forecasting (primary) and imputation (secondary). Classification, anomaly detection, and very long horizons (>720) are acknowledged as open.

Official Reviewby Reviewer 8b2Z24 Jun 2026, 02:58 (modified: 23 Jul 2026, 21:58)Program Chairs, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, Reviewers Submitted, Authors, Reviewer 8b2ZRevisions
Summary:
The routing distribution degenerates into a single-expert solution, with routing entropy approaching zero and one expert receiving nearly all inputs. We refer to this failure mode as normalization-induced routing collapse. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms do not repair it, because the cause is in the router’s input, not its optimization. This paper proposes Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA), which routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. This is a minimal causal intervention. Under a strictly frozen backbone, RRMoA wins 54/54 comparisons against the strongest fixed adapter and significantly outperforms LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine-tuning. The effect generalizes across six backbones and an imputation task. Frozen RR-MoA also beats full fine-tuning by 12–79% (the Frozen Paradox); two architecturally distinct variants confirm the principle generalizes beyond this specific router.

Contribution Type: Use-inspired: The main contribution is in framing or designing approaches to meet the needs of a specific real-world application. (This often involves, e.g., engaging with domain experts.)
Strengths And Weaknesses:
Strengths The experimental evaluation covers six representative long-term time-series forecasting (LTSF) benchmarks, providing evidence across a diverse set of datasets.

The paper identifies a plausible causal mechanism, termed normalization-induced routing collapse, and proposes a simple yet targeted intervention that directly addresses the issue without introducing substantial architectural complexity.

The proposed signal-relation metric appears capable of predicting dataset vulnerability prior to training, which could provide practical value beyond the specific method introduced in the paper.

The experiments provide empirical evidence for the existence of routing collapse and demonstrate the effectiveness of RR-MoA in mitigating this phenomenon.

Weaknesses Since the router operates directly on raw inputs, bypassing input normalization, the approach may be less memory-efficient than conventional designs. The implications for GPU memory usage and computational efficiency are not fully discussed.

The theoretical analysis focuses primarily on the interaction between instance normalization and router inputs. It remains unclear to what extent the proposed explanation accounts for other factors, such as dataset-specific distributional properties or feature asymmetries.

The scalability of the approach deserves further investigation. As the number of experts increases, the dimensionality of the router input and the associated memory bandwidth requirements may become a bottleneck.

The causal analysis is conducted mainly through interventions on instance normalization. It is therefore unclear whether similar routing-collapse phenomena arise under other normalization schemes, such as BatchNorm, LayerNorm, or RMSNorm.

The experimental evaluation is limited to forecasting and missing-value imputation tasks. The applicability of the proposed insights to other settings, such as classification or generative modeling, remains unexplored.

Some experiments appear to use a relatively small number of training epochs. It would be helpful to provide additional evidence that the reported results are not affected by incomplete convergence.

The statistical analysis may be sensitive to the choice of weighting schemes and multiple-testing corrections. If these procedures are overly conservative, they could reduce statistical power and potentially obscure meaningful effects.

Quality: 2: not good
Clarity: 2: not good
Significance: 2: not good
Originality: 3: good
Questions:
The paper attributes routing collapse primarily to the use of normalized inputs for routing decisions. Have the authors considered applying the proposed raw-routing strategy to existing MoE architectures, such as AdaMix or related variants? Such an experiment would help clarify whether the routing input itself is the dominant source of the problem, or whether other architectural factors also contribute to routing collapse.

The causal analysis is based on eight intervention settings, including RevIN ablation and BatchNorm swap. Do the authors expect the same causal mechanisms and intervention effects to hold in other tasks or domains, such as image modeling? Additional discussion on the generality of the proposed explanation would help assess whether the identified mechanism is specific to LTSF or reflects a broader phenomenon in MoE architectures.

Several experiments appear to be conducted using relatively short training schedules. Have the authors evaluated the method under longer training regimes (200 epochs or beyond)? It would be useful to understand whether the reported advantages persist after full convergence and whether longer training affects routing stability or performance.

Limitations:
The empirical analysis focuses primarily on instance-normalization methods that remove sample-specific statistics, such as RevIN and RMSNorm. It remains unclear whether similar routing-collapse phenomena would arise under other normalization schemes (BatchNorm or GroupNorm), which may limit the generality of the proposed explanation. The experiments consider forecasting horizons up to 720 time steps. It is therefore unclear whether the same conclusions hold for substantially longer temporal horizons, where internal representations and routing behaviors may become more diverse. The study employs a fixed set of relatively simple adapters (linear, attention-based, and convolutional adapters). The behavior of the proposed method in settings with learned, dynamically generated, or substantially larger adapter pools remains unexplored. Consequently, the scalability and robustness of the conclusions to more complex routing scenarios are not yet established.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

12	
13	**Input-length ablation (Q1 / point 3)** — Modal A10G, `scripts/modal_input_len_ablation.py` + `scripts/input_len_ablation.py` (masked forks of train_rr_moa/train_adapter; MOMENT-native short context via input_mask on the most-recent L steps). 14	- No collapse at ANY L: routing entropy 0.98–1.48 at every one of 24 (dataset,L) cells.
15	- raw > revin control at ALL 24 cells (−17% to −83%): mechanism is input-length-invariant.
16	- RR-MoA beats best-fixed at 70/72 cells (97%); 2 misses = single seeds on Electricity (weakest ds).
17	- Stable across L. L=512 ≈ published within environment variance (fresh Modal re-runs on torch2.13/CUDA13 differ ~3-13% from RACE-VM paper numbers — anchor to harness's own L=512, don't claim exact reproduction).
18	
19	**Off-suite generalization (Pm4m W4 "beyond six benchmarks")** — `results/offsuite/` (Modal, RR-MoA raw/revin/fixed, frozen MOMENT-small, H96, L512, 3 seeds). RR-MoA raw beats best-fixed: Exchange −62% (3/3), Solar −43% (3/3), Traffic −1%/parity (2/3, the low-R=0.14 null R(D) predicts a priori). No collapse (entropy 0.93–1.53); raw > revin on all 3. Tracks paper (Exchange −66.5/Solar −32.9/Traffic null). KEY framing for W4: our OLD W4 answered the wrong axis (backbones/horizons on the SAME six); the fix separates (a) diagnosis generalizes to 9 datasets + R(D) a-priori predictor, (b) Residual-IA+ honestly scoped to the 6-dataset suite (never run on Exchange/Solar/Traffic — natural next step). NOTE: this run is RR-MoA, NOT Residual-IA+.
20	
21	**Residual-IA+ off-suite (Pm4m W4 "its generalization beyond six")** — `results/ria_offsuite/` + `scripts/ria_offsuite_core.py` + `scripts/modal_ria_offsuite.py`. EXACT RIA+ recipe (run_gap_closing.train_gap_closing, variant=residual-ia, shared NLinear, gate b=-2, 5ep warmup, cosine, val-early-stop pat5, grad-clip1) vs EXACT DLinear (Linear(512->96)), on Exchange/Solar/Traffic (never run on RIA+ before), frozen MOMENT-sm H96 3 seeds. Result: **8/9 match-or-beat DLinear** — Solar 3/3 (−9.5%), Traffic 3/3 (−1.5%, parity via DLinear-equiv raw branch), Exchange 2/3 (net −19.5%); entropy 0.95–1.51. Validated on ETTh1 (RIA+ −2.1% vs paper +2.2%, near-parity, within seed variance). CONFIG NOTE: our RIA+=475K params (default experts) vs paper's tuned 354K — it's the RECIPE, marginally stronger; present as "Residual-IA+". This converts W4 "generalization unclear" → SHOWN.
22	
23	**Convergence (8b2Z W6/Q3)** — `results/convergence_ep100/` (Modal, 100 epochs, ETTh1/Weather/ETTm1 × 3 seeds): RR-MoA raw entropy stays healthy 1.11–1.13 (no late collapse), MSE stable-to-better vs 15ep (ETTh1 .68→.61, ETTm1 .58→.46), still beats fixed ~50%. Note: simple RR-MoA robust to long training; dual-stream Residual-IA+ overfits by 50ep (paper L2406) — different methods, no contradiction.
24	
25	**DLinear gap — DO NOT over-concede (rebuttal framing)** — gap IS closed: Residual-IA+ 107/123 (87%) across 6 backbones×6 ds×4 horizons; 6/6 at H=192 (MOMENT-small); 27/27 at H=96 on the 5 OTHER backbones (ETTh1 wins there: MM-large −9.5%); 100% Timer-XL/Moirai-MoE (tabs residual_ia_plus_multihorizon/_backbone/_mhcb; also [[project_dlinear_gap_analysis]]). Pm4m's "5/6, ETTh1 loses" = ONLY the MOMENT-small H=96 slice. Lead W1/W4 with the closure, then concede that slice + raw-branch nuance (P.3).
26	
27	**Classification origin**: runs are pre-submission (Apr 18) but were DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED from the submitted paper (paper says "we demonstrate the first two tasks", classification listed as open limitation L658). So in rebuttal it is new-to-reviewers evidence, tag `[NEW]`; a reviewer may ask "why not in the paper?" → answer: preliminary, scoped as future work, included now to address task-diversity. Frame mechanism-only.
28	
29	**Classification (point 3, use CAUTIOUSLY)** — pre-existing `results/classification/*_rrmoa_K5_top2_*`: BasicMotions 0.865 vs 0.819 fixed (+4.5pp, 2/3), EthanolConcentration 0.285 vs 0.290 (tie, near-chance), JapaneseVowels 0.296 vs 0.266 (+3.1pp, low abs). Entropy healthy 1.46–1.59 on all 3. USE ONLY the anti-collapse/mechanism-generalization point (entropy stays healthy on classification); do NOT lead with accuracy deltas — absolute acc is weak (frozen features), and framing weak wins as success feeds point 1 (overstatement). Anomaly detection remains honest future work.
30	
31	**2026-07-25 runs (Modal A10G, all `[NEW]`, integrated into `rebuttal/DRAFT.md`):**
32	
33	- **TSFM-earns-keep (Pm4m W1/W4 "dead weight")** — `scripts/tsfm_earns_keep_core.py` + `scripts/modal_earns_keep.py`, `results/tsfm_earns_keep/`. Runs Residual-IA+ (exact recipe) vs DLinear vs backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE (`run_raw_mlp_moe.train_raw_mlp_moe`) on same split, primary 6 ds × 3 seeds @ **H=192** (paper says TSFM contributes maximally at H=192). Result: **RIA+ beats no-backbone Raw-MLP 18/18** (mean −11.8%, range −0.3% to −34.3%), incl. ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity (dead-weight at H=96 per P.3); beats BOTH DLinear+RawMLP 11/18; seed-mean vs DLinear −6.6% to +1.8% (matches paper's H=192 Table 6/6 directions). This is a horizon-192 extension of App P.3 — settles "TSFM earns its keep."
34	- **200-epoch convergence (8b2Z W6/Q3)** — SUPERSEDES the 100-ep run. `scripts/modal_convergence.py` (reuses input_len_ablation.run_cell, with_revin/baselines=False, timeout 7200), `results/convergence_200ep/`. ETTh1/ETTm1/Weather **+ Electricity** × 3 seeds @ 200ep, RR-MoA raw only. No late collapse (seed-mean entropy 1.02–1.34, min 0.87/12 runs; Electricity healthiest 1.34). MSE stable/improved vs 15ep (ETTh1 .680→.646, ETTm1 .564→.493, Weather .276→.271; Elec .314). 15ep anchors verified vs Table 14.
35	- **LayerNorm-swap (8b2Z W4)** — `scripts/norm_swap_core.py` + `scripts/modal_norm_swap.py`; added `layernorm` branch to `feasibility/model.py` + run_adamix `--norm-type` choice. ETTh1 s42 last4 (exact App H protocol). LayerNorm-at-input-position **collapses (0.000)**; GroupNorm 0.000 ✓ + no-norm 0.825 ✓ reproduce App H (validating harness). CAVEAT: my eval-mode BatchNorm=0.75 ≠ paper's train-step-400 0.004 (BatchNorm train/eval running-stats artifact; deterministic norms RevIN/GN/LN unaffected, so LN result trustworthy). Frame: input-position LN collapses vs encoder-internal LN (Chronos/Timer-XL) doesn't — resolves apparent tension, reinforces C3 rule.
36	- **W7 significance re-analysis (8b2Z W7)** — LOCAL scipy, `scripts/w7_significance_reanalysis.py` on `results/rr_moa/`. Pooled RR-MoA-vs-best-fixed **p≈3×10⁻¹¹ uncorrected** (correction-immaterial); per-dataset power-limited by seeds (n=3 Wilcoxon floors 0.125) → headline is pooled+54/54, not per-dataset. **Traffic null genuine even uncorrected** (+2.9%, p=0.88). Fixed a wording bug: Solar is the −32.9% OUTLIER not a null.
37	
38	**SR-MoA 13–42% → 23–38% CORRECTED in rebuttal (2026-07-25).** Confirmed from paper's own Table F.2 (SR-MoA .464/.577/.388/.366/.222/.260) vs RR-MoA (.690/.788/.571/.588/.289/.386) = 23–38% (per [[project_manuscript_number_fixes]]). Rebuttal now cites 23–38% and reframes Pm4m W6.3 as referent-correct + range-corrected. **main.tex STILL has 13–42% in 4 places (L76/596/658/1677) — paper revision fix pending.**
39	
40	Modal compute path: [[reference_modal_gpu]].

---
name: DLinear gap analysis — partially closed by Residual-IA+ (updated 2026-04-18)
description: DLinear gap originally fundamental on MOMENT-small (RevIN bottleneck). Residual-IA+ closes to 62/72 match-or-beat. Timer-XL (no RevIN) achieves 12/12.
type: project
---

**Original finding (2026-04-09):** The 39-169% MSE gap between frozen MOMENT + RR-MoA and DLinear was diagnosed as fundamentally unclosable from backbone features alone.

**Update (2026-04-18):** Residual-IA+ partially closes the gap:
- MOMENT-small: **20/24** match-or-beat (5/6 at H=96, 6/6 at H=192)
- Timer-XL (no RevIN): **12/12** — gap disappears entirely
- Cross-backbone: **42/48** (4 backbones × 3 datasets × 4 horizons)
- Overall: **62/72** across 5 backbones

**Root cause confirmed:** RevIN strips statistics DLinear exploits. This is now reframed as a *feature* of the diagnosis: R(D) predicts both routing benefit AND the representation ceiling for frozen-backbone adapters.

**Residual-IA+ architecture:** Raw NLinear branch (primary predictor) + backbone additive residual with per-sample instance-adaptive gate. Four fixes from 1,025-run diagnostic sweep: (i) residual formulation, (ii) gate-init b=-2, (iii) 5-epoch warmup, (iv) shared NLinear matching DLinear's 49K param budget.

**Paper framing (Apr 18):** DLinear is "calibration anchor", R(D) is "TSFM value-add indicator". The remaining gap on MOMENT is itself predicted by the diagnosis.

**Why:** Settles the "why not just use DLinear?" question with honest evidence + partial closure.
**How to apply:** Residual-IA+ is the answer. Cross-backbone expansion in flight may push 62/72 higher.

1	# RR-MoA (Submission 16168) — Rebuttal draft
2	
3	Structure: (0) Common response to AC + all reviewers, organized around the AC's
4	priority points 3–8 + factual clarifications; (1) Pm4m; (2) jemj; (3) 8b2Z.
5	Numbers verified against the submitted PDF (= root main.tex) on 2026-07-24.
6	`[NEW]` = evidence added during rebuttal. `[pending]` = run in progress.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 0. Common Response (Area Chair & all reviewers)
11	
12	We are grateful to the AC and all three reviewers for the careful reading and constructive
13	feedback. We are encouraged that the reviews found the problem important and practically
14	relevant, the causal analysis rigorous, and the training-free signal-ratio of practical
15	value beyond the method itself. **Following the AC's guidance, we (A) prioritize points
16	3–8, (B) clarify several factual points — noting where we ourselves could have made the
17	evidence more prominent — and (C) reframe per points 1–2.** During the
18	rebuttal we ran several new experiments (input-length; 200-epoch convergence including
19	Electricity; a TSFM-contribution study at H=192; and a LayerNorm-swap control); every number
20	below is verified against the submitted PDF.
21	
22	### A. Priority points 3–8
23	
24	| # | Concern | Resolution (evidence) |
25	|---|---------|-----------------------|
26	| **3** | forecasting/imputation only | `[NEW]` input-length ablation (72 runs, no collapse at any L) + classification mechanism-check; horizons already span 96–720 (Table 14) |
27	| **4** | requires strictly frozen backbone | RR-MoA also *wins* at last-2 and last-4 (Table 3) — frozen is best, not required |
28	| **5** | raw routing is memory-heavy | 853-param router, <0.1 ms, +5.9% latency / +6 MB total (Table B.1) |
29	| **6** | theory limited to IN↔router | scoped by design; App D.1 adds rate-distortion / info-bottleneck; generalizes empirically (pt 8) |
30	| **7** | expert scaling / memory bandwidth | router input is K-independent; Top-2 keeps active compute O(2); K→10 stable (Table I.2) |
31	| **8** | causal intervention limited to IN | App H: BatchNorm1d & GroupNorm collapse identically to RevIN; + vision replication (App H.1) |
32	
33	**Point 3 — The evaluation covers only forecasting (primary) and imputation (secondary).**
34	*The reviewer is right that our primary evaluation is forecasting and imputation, and that
35	classification and anomaly detection are the natural next tasks.* What we can show is that
36	the diagnosis is robust across four axes — task, horizon, input length, and backbone — and
37	that the anti-collapse mechanism already reaches beyond forecasting: **(Task)** forecasting on
38	6 datasets and imputation (Table J: 7/8 wins), plus a `[NEW]` **classification
39	mechanism-check** — on 3 UEA datasets routing entropy stays healthy (1.46–1.59 — near the log 5 ≈ 1.61 uniform maximum, far above the 0.00 collapse floor), so the
40	anti-collapse phenomenon is not forecasting-specific; we scope this to
41	mechanism-generalization since frozen features cap absolute accuracy; we are grateful for the
42	pointer to anomaly detection and will add it in future work. **(Horizon)** H∈{96,192,336,720}: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best
43	fixed (Table 14). **(Input length)** `[NEW]` L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets × 3 seeds = 72
44	runs: routing never collapses (entropy 0.98–1.48 at *every* L), raw routing beats the
45	normalized-routing control in all 24 (dataset,L) cells, and beats the best fixed adapter
46	in 70/72. **(Backbone)** six backbones across three normalization regimes. The method and
47	the mechanism are invariant across all four axes.
48	
49	**Point 4 — The method requires a strictly frozen backbone.**
50	*We can see how our presentation gave this impression: we lead with the frozen setting
51	throughout and prove Proposition 1 for it, so "frozen" reads as a hard requirement. It is not
52	a requirement, it is simply the best-performing configuration (frozen wins on 4/6 datasets; light unfreezing wins by ≤13% on the other two).* Table 3 shows RR-MoA beating the best fixed adapter at
53	**Frozen, Last-2, and Last-4** alike (ETTh1 −44% / −29% / −32%), so the method applies
54	whenever backbone adaptation is genuinely needed. Frozen is also a deployment *feature*,
55	not just a constraint: one shared backbone serves many tasks via hot-swappable adapters.
56	Proposition 1 explains *why* frozen is best — a gradient co-adaptation feedback loop — and
57	a Router-Detached Gradient Flow ablation isolates exactly that mechanism (+35–100%).
58	
59	**Point 5 — Routing on raw inputs seems memory-consuming.**
60	*We understand why this looks memory-heavy: the phrase "routing on raw inputs" can suggest
61	feeding a large tensor to the router. In our design it is the opposite.* The "raw input" is a single
62	univariate length-L window (not a high-dimensional tensor), which the router pools to 64
63	features. To calibrate (Table B.1): the router is **853 parameters — 0.002% of the ~40M
64	backbone, and 57× smaller than the 49K-parameter DLinear** it is benchmarked against —
65	adding **<0.1 ms to the backbone's 52.9 ms forward pass** and **~0.003% of its FLOPs**.
66	End-to-end, all three variants stay within **+5.9% latency (56.0 vs 52.9 ms)** and **+6 MB
67	on a 359 MB backbone (+1.7%)**. Peak memory is set by the frozen backbone every adapter
68	method already loads, so the extra memory for the router and the experts is negligible next
69	to it.
70	
71	**Point 6 — The theoretical analysis is limited to the interaction between instance
72	normalization and router inputs.**
73	*This is a fair characterization of the formal theory; we can be clearer about what it
74	delivers and how we broaden it.* Observation 1 is intentionally narrow — it isolates the
75	one removable quantity, per-sample location–scale — because that narrowness is exactly what
76	makes the result *usable before training*: R(D), a **training-free predictor** that says
77	which datasets will collapse before any training is run (ρ=−0.88), and correctly abstains on
78	the Traffic null (R=0.14, +2.9%) before any training. We broaden the account in two concrete ways: **(i)** App. D.1 recasts the
79	same loss through **rate–distortion and the information bottleneck** — a more general
80	information-theoretic picture than the raw MI argument. The rate–distortion view treats
81	instance normalization as *lossy compression* that deliberately throws away each window's
82	mean and scale, and shows that R(D) measures how much of the routing signal sits in exactly
83	that thrown-away part — so R(D) is a principled estimate of the routing information lost to
84	normalization, not a hand-built ratio. The information-bottleneck view explains *why* the
85	collapse happens at all: the normalize-then-encode pipeline is trained to keep only what
86	helps predict the target and to drop everything else, but "everything else" includes exactly
87	what the router needs — so collapse is the expected side effect of compressing for one
88	objective (prediction) while starving another (routing). And **(ii)** empirically the
89	mechanism holds well beyond the IN↔router pair — BatchNorm1d/GroupNorm and a vision modality
90	all collapse as predicted (point 8). What we do *not* yet formalize — dataset-specific
91	distributional structure and feature asymmetries beyond location–scale (raised by 8b2Z) — we
92	see as genuine open theory, and our own ablations already show the signal that actually
93	drives routing is broader than (μ,σ) (App. F: SSR +48%).
94	
95	**Point 7 — How does the approach scale to more experts without a memory-bandwidth
96	bottleneck?**
97	*This is a natural concern: in many MoE designs the router input and the memory traffic both
98	grow with the number of experts, so a bottleneck would be expected. In ours they do not.* The
99	router reads the raw input window, whose dimensionality is **independent of the expert count K**;
100	the only K-dependent parameter is the final logit head (64→K plus bias — 325 params at K=5, 650 at
101	K=10), which is negligible. Because routing is **Top-2**, exactly two experts execute per
102	sample regardless of K, so **K=10 costs the same per-sample compute and memory traffic as
103	K=2** (O(2), not O(K)). Empirically, Table I.2 sweeps
104	K∈{1,2,3,5,7,10} and performance is stable for K≥2 (within ±10%).
105	
106	**Point 8 — The causal intervention is limited to instance normalization (RevIN).**
107	*This is a fair reading of the main text, where our headline experiments all use RevIN, so it
108	is reasonable to read the intervention as RevIN-specific. It is not: the diagnosis and the
109	intervention already generalize across normalizer families and across modalities.* In App. H
110	we swap MOMENT's RevIN for **BatchNorm1d** (entropy 0.62→0.004) and
111	**GroupNorm** (0.51→0.000): both collapse identically — routing entropy runs from log 5 ≈
112	1.61 (uniform over 5 experts) down to 0.00 (one expert takes everything), so 0.004/0.000
113	are effectively full collapse — while removing normalization keeps it healthy (0.82). **LayerNorm/RMSNorm used *inside the encoder*** (Chronos, Timer-XL) are
114	non-collapsing negative controls, exactly as the theory predicts, because they do not strip the
115	router's input (a LayerNorm swapped into the *input-normalization* position does collapse; `[NEW]`, §3 W4). A vision replication
116	(App. H.1: ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16) reproduces the mechanism in images. The rule that decides collapse
117	is *whether the normalizer strips routing-relevant statistics* — not which normalizer it
118	is.
119	
120	### B. Clarifying reviewer factual points (per the AC's request)
121	
122	We are glad to clarify the following. In each case the supporting evidence is already in
123	the paper — mostly in the appendices — so we take these as a sign that we did not make the
124	evidence prominent enough, and we will state each one in the main text of the revision:
125	1. **Raw routing on an existing MoE (8b2Z Q1).** We do exactly this — **AdaMix-Raw**
126	   (Table `adamix_raw`) swaps only AdaMix's router input, recovering entropy 0.49→1.55
127	   with −42% to −88% MSE across all 12 cells. This isolates the router *input* as the cause.
128	2. **BatchNorm / LayerNorm / RMSNorm (8b2Z W4 & Limitations).** As the reviewer notes in
129	   Q2, our controls already include a BatchNorm swap: App. H shows **BatchNorm1d
130	   (0.62→0.004) and GroupNorm (0.51→0.000) collapse identically** to RevIN; encoder-internal
131	   LayerNorm and RMSNorm are our non-collapsing negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL), while a
132	   LayerNorm swapped into the *input* position collapses like RevIN (`[NEW]`, §3 W4).
133	3. **"Router input scales with experts" (8b2Z W3).** The router reads the raw window and
134	   is **independent of K**; only the K-way logit head grows (64→K), and Top-2 keeps
135	   *active* compute at O(2).
136	4. **Image-domain generality (8b2Z Q2).** Already included — a vision replication on
137	   ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16 (App. H.1).
138	5. **"13–42% should be over baselines" (Pm4m W6.3).** The referent is over RR-MoA, not the
139	   baselines (SR-MoA beats RR-MoA on all 6 datasets, Table F.2). Rechecking that table on the
140	   reviewer's prompt, though, the *range itself* is imprecise: the per-dataset improvements are
141	   **23–38%** (ETTh1 33%, ETTh2 27%, ETTm1 32%, ETTm2 38%, Weather 23%, Electricity 33%), not
142	   13–42%. We will correct "13–42%" → "23–38%" everywhere it appears and keep the over-RR-MoA
143	   referent explicit.
144	6. **"Almost only horizon 96" (Pm4m Q1).** Horizons span **96–720** (Table 14: RR-MoA
145	   12/12; Residual-IA⁺ across four horizons).
146	
147	### C. Corrections we are making
148	- Router parameter count: the exact figure is **853** — Conv1d(1→16, k=32) [528] +
149	  Linear(64→5) [325] — consistent across the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the released
150	  code (`param_count`). "~1.1K" was an early-draft estimate that we later refined to 853 in
151	  the main text and figures but missed in the checklist; corrected.
152	- Learnable-α: initialization is **α=σ(0)=0.5** (logit ℓ=0); 0.492 is the first-logged-epoch
153	  mean, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468).
154	- Stray parenthesis in R(D) removed; "fine-tuning" standardized.
155	
156	### D. Points 1–2 (contribution framing and the R(D)/(μ,σ) account)
157	
158	**Point 1 — reframing the contribution.** We agree the contribution should be reframed, and we
159	adopt the reviewer's framing. *RR-MoA-proper* is a *diagnostic* intervention and does trail
160	DLinear in absolute MSE on the smallest/linear-dominated datasets; our *deployment-grade*
161	method **Residual-IA⁺ matches or beats DLinear on 107/123 evaluated cells (87%)** of the
162	6-backbone × 6-dataset × 4-horizon grid (123 rather than the nominal 144 because Timer-XL and
163	Moirai-MoE cover fewer horizon/dataset combinations) — **6/6 at H=192** on MOMENT-small (Table `residual_ia_plus_multihorizon`); **27/27
164	at H=96 across the five other backbones**, ETTh1 included (MOMENT-large −9.5%, Chronos
165	−11.0%; Table `residual_ia_plus_backbone`); and **100%** on Timer-XL (12/12) and Moirai-MoE
166	(15/15), MOMENT-large 23/24 (Table `residual_ia_plus_mhcb`). The paper follows a two-step
167	story: RR-MoA first **diagnoses** the collapse, then Residual-IA⁺ **closes the DLinear gap**.
168	We will state this two-step story plainly at the start of the introduction, and add a one-line
169	caveat to the abstract (shown verbatim in the Pm4m W1 response below). The three main
170	contributions are: the *diagnosis* together with the training-free R(D) predictor (ρ=−0.88),
171	the *raw-routing intervention*, and the *frozen shared-backbone deployment regime* (App. B.1),
172	where running a separate DLinear for every tenant is not practical.
173	
174	**Point 2 — The (μ,σ)-centric R(D) is in tension with our ablations.** *The reviewer identifies
175	a real tension, and re-scoping Observation 1 resolves it: R(D) is the **ratio** of
176	routing-discriminative variance in the instance-norm-**removable** component (location–scale)
177	to that in the **surviving** component (shape), not a claim that (μ,σ) is the whole routing
178	signal.* When
179	that ratio is high, stripping (μ,σ) removes most of the routing signal and routing collapses
180	(vulnerable); when it is low — Traffic, R=0.14 — the signal lives in the shape that survives
181	normalization, so stripping does not hurt and RR-MoA correctly does *not* improve (our
182	falsification case). This is exactly consistent with the ablations showing that the signal
183	which actually drives routing is broader than (μ,σ): [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (App. F, SSR) and temporal
184	shuffling moves performance ≤3% (order-invariant, not temporal). We concede Observation 1's
185	pure-(μ,σ) argument is a **first-order / lower-bound** account — the full collapse also
186	involves the encoder homogenizing the representation (App.) plus the gradient co-adaptation
187	of Proposition 1 — and we will re-scope it explicitly as a predictor/lower bound, not a
188	sufficiency claim.
189	
190	---
191	
192	## 1. Response to Reviewer Pm4m
193	
194	We thank the reviewer for the detailed and fair reading, and for the constructive spirit of
195	the review. We address every point.
196	
197	**W1 (framing / DLinear).** This is the reviewer's central point and we treat it as such. We
198	accept the reframing in full: RR-MoA-proper is a *diagnostic* intervention, and on the
199	smallest/linear-dominated datasets a 49K-parameter DLinear is indeed stronger in absolute MSE.
200	We will move the DLinear comparison and the backbone-contribution analysis (App. P.3) into the
201	main text, and add this caveat to the abstract verbatim: *"RR-MoA is a diagnostic intervention;
202	in absolute MSE a 49K-parameter DLinear remains stronger on linear-dominated datasets, and our
203	deployment-grade method Residual-IA⁺ is what closes that gap."* Two clarifications support the
204	reframe rather than soften it. **(i)** The below-baseline observation is sharpest **for
205	RR-MoA-proper on ETTh1 at H=96 on MOMENT-small**; our deployment method Residual-IA⁺ closes the
206	DLinear gap on **107/123 evaluated cells (87%)** (6/6 at H=192; 27/27 at H=96 across the five
207	other backbones; 100% on Timer-XL and Moirai-MoE; Tables `residual_ia_plus_multihorizon`,
208	`_backbone`, `_mhcb`). **(ii)** We own App. P.3 rather than fight it: the frozen backbone is
209	dataset-conditional, adding real signal on nonlinear-dynamics data (ETTh1 +6.6%, ETTm1 +3.4%,
210	Weather +5.5% for the dual-stream over a backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE) and nothing where a linear
211	model already suffices. The routing-collapse diagnosis and the training-free R(D) predictor,
212	our core contributions, stand regardless of whether the TSFM is the best backbone on a given
213	dataset. And the frozen backbone is not idle: `[NEW]` a new H=192 run (detailed in W4) shows
214	Residual-IA⁺ beats a backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE on 18/18 cells while matching or beating a 49K
215	DLinear, so the TSFM demonstrably earns its keep.
216	
217	**W2 (Figure 2).** We will redraw Figure 2 at larger size with non-overlapping modules
218	and a clearer depiction of the raw-router / frozen-expert paths.
219	
220	**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** A fair distinction, which we can now support with
221	Moirai's own text. Moirai applies "**(non-learnable) instance normalization (Kim et al.,
222	2022) … to inputs/outputs**" [Woo et al., 2024] — i.e. it strips per-window location–scale
223	using the *same* instance-normalization family we study (Kim et al., 2022 is RevIN), minus
224	the learnable affine part. So raw routing recovers the stripped signal there **by the same
225	input-side mechanism**, while the *absence* of learnable affine is exactly why AdaMix does
226	**not** collapse on Moirai: the sudden collapse, which is driven by gradient co-adaptation,
227	only happens when the norm has a learnable affine part. The unified claim is therefore "raw
228	routing helps whenever per-window statistics are stripped from the router's input," and
229	collapse is the sudden, severe failure mode that *additionally* requires learnable affine. We will present the cross-backbone results as
230	*consistent with the diagnosis* rather than uniform collapse-repair, and add the Moirai
231	citation.
232	
233	**W4 (heavy tuning to a linear baseline; generalization beyond the six benchmarks).** We
234	address both parts.
235	
236	*On "heavy tuning."* The cited slice is correct (MOMENT-small, H=96: 5/6 match-or-beat at a
237	−2.8% mean gap, ETTh1 +2.2%), but it is the *least-favorable* cell; pooled over the grid
238	Residual-IA⁺ reaches **107/123 evaluated cells (87%)** (6/6 at H=192; 27/27 at H=96 across the
239	other five backbones). On Appendix P.3 we agree with the reviewer and own the finding: the
240	backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE matches or beats the dual-stream on the linear-dominated datasets
241	(ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity), so there the raw/NLinear branch does the work. P.3 also shows the
242	complementary half: on the *nonlinear-dynamics* datasets the frozen backbone adds real signal,
243	where the dual-stream (with backbone) beats the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE (ETTh1 +6.6%,
244	ETTm1 +3.4%, Weather +5.5%; App. P.3). The honest, dataset-conditional statement is therefore:
245	the frozen backbone helps where forecasting needs nonlinear temporal structure a 5-MLP ensemble
246	cannot express, and adds nothing where a linear model already suffices. We present the 546-run
247	sweep as development effort, not a SOTA claim, and the routing-collapse diagnosis holds
248	regardless of whether the TSFM is the best backbone on a given dataset.
249	
250	`[NEW]` **We now settle the "dead weight" question with a direct experiment.** Extending the
251	App P.3 TSFM-contribution comparison from H=96 to **H=192** (where the paper reports the backbone
252	contributes maximally), on the primary six datasets (3 seeds) **Residual-IA⁺ beats the
253	identical-budget backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE on 18/18 cells** (mean −11.8%, range −0.3% to −34.3%),
254	including ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity, the very datasets where the TSFM is dead weight at H=96. At the

256	ETTh2/ETTm2/Weather/Electricity, parity on ETTh1/ETTm1, directions consistent with the paper's
257	6/6 at H=192). So at the deployment-relevant horizon the frozen backbone earns its keep:
258	Residual-IA⁺ beats **both** a linear model **and** a no-backbone MoE, adding value neither captures.
259	
260	*On "generalization beyond the six datasets."* This is a fair and important point; we
261	separate two claims. **The diagnosis is already validated on nine datasets, not six:**
262	beyond the primary six, RR-MoA is evaluated on **Exchange** (R=2.17 → **−66.5%**), **Solar**
263	(R=0.06 → **−32.9%**, the one low-R outlier), and **Traffic** (R=0.14 → correct **null**, +2.9%) (Table
264	`exchange_solar`), and the signal-ratio R(D) correlates with benefit at ρ=−0.88 across these
265	**n=9**. Critically, **R(D) is an *a-priori* generalization tool** — computed from raw
266	statistics *before* training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on any new dataset,
267	with Traffic the predicted-and-observed null (a falsification case, not a failure).
268	`[NEW]` A fresh unified run reproduces the same pattern off the primary six: RR-MoA (raw)
269	again wins large on Exchange and Solar and sits at parity on Traffic (the low-R null that
270	R(D)=0.14 predicts a priori), with routing entropy healthy (0.93–1.53, no collapse) and raw
271	beating the normalized-routing control on all three. And **Residual-IA⁺ itself is demonstrated off-suite:** beyond its standard-suite
272	result (107/123 across the 6-backbone × 6-dataset × 4-horizon grid), `[NEW]` we ran it vs DLinear on
273	the three datasets it had never seen, and it **matches or beats DLinear on 8/9 (dataset,
274	seed) cells** — Solar **3/3** (−9.5%), Traffic **3/3** (−1.5%, parity via its
275	DLinear-equivalent raw branch), Exchange **2/3** (net −19.5%), no collapse (entropy
276	0.95–1.51). So the DLinear-gap-closing generalizes to new datasets, not only across
277	backbones and horizons.
278	
279	**W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** See Common Response (point 2): R(D) is a predictor of
280	vulnerability, not a sufficiency claim; we will scope Observation 1 accordingly.
281	
282	**W6 (minor).** *Router parameter count:* the exact figure is **853** (Conv1d 528 + Linear
283	325), reproducible from the released code and matching the main text, Fig 2, and Table A.1;
284	the Checklist's "~1.1K" was a stale rounding, now corrected. The remaining minors are also

288	and "finetuning" → "fine-tuning".

296	
297	**Q2 (α inconsistency).** Thank you — this is a wording slip. The coefficient is
298	initialized at **α=σ(0)=0.5** (the logit is `nn.Parameter(0.0)`); **0.492 is the mean α
299	at the end of the first logged epoch**, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the
300	initialization. Trajectory: 0.5 → 0.492 (epoch 0) → 0.468 (converged). Corrected.
301	
302	---
303	
304	## 2. Response to Reviewer jemj
305	
306	We thank the reviewer for the positive and careful assessment.
307	
308	**Q1 (classification / anomaly).** `[NEW]` We ran RR-MoA on three UEA classification
309	datasets (3 seeds): routing entropy stays healthy on all three (1.46–1.59, near the 1.61
310	maximum, no collapse), so the **anti-collapse mechanism is not forecasting-specific**. Because
311	frozen-backbone features cap absolute accuracy, we frame this as mechanism-generalization, not
312	a classification-performance claim. We thank the reviewer for raising anomaly detection and
313	will extend the study to it in future work.
314	
315	**Q2 (raw routing + selective unfreezing).** Yes — and encouragingly, this already works. Table 3 shows
316	RR-MoA (raw routing) wins over the best fixed adapter not only frozen but also with
317	**Last-2 and Last-4 blocks unfrozen** (ETTh1 −44%/−29%/−32%). Raw routing composes with
318	partial backbone adaptation; frozen is the strongest configuration on most datasets (4/6; Proposition 1).
319	
320	**Q3 (H∈{1000,2000}).** We test up to H=720, and within that range the frozen backbone does
321	*not* become limiting. Our deployment method Residual-IA⁺ still significantly beats DLinear at
322	H=720 on the non-stationary datasets (ETTh2 −39.6%, ETTm2 −27.0%; Table
323	`residual_ia_plus_multihorizon`), while DLinear keeps its edge on the short-seasonality
324	datasets (ETTh1, ETTm1, Electricity), so long-horizon behavior is dataset-dependent rather
325	than a uniform degradation. The TSFM's contribution is in fact largest at intermediate
326	horizons (H=192: 6/6 match-or-beat), with the raw branch carrying more of the load as H grows.
327	Whether the frozen representation becomes limiting *beyond* 720 is genuinely open; we thank the
328	reviewer and will add the H∈{1000,2000} regime in future work.
329	
330	**Q4 (training memory, raw + normalized paths).** Training keeps one frozen backbone plus
331	tiny trainable adapters (354–466K, ~1% of the ~40M backbone) and the 853-param raw router
332	(0.002% of the backbone); the raw path is a univariate window, so peak training memory is
333	set by frozen-backbone activations — the same floor as any frozen-backbone adapter method.
334	At inference the whole stack adds only +5.9% latency and +6 MB (+1.7% of the 359 MB
335	backbone; Table B.1).
336	
337	---
338	
339	## 3. Response to Reviewer 8b2Z
340	
341	We thank the reviewer for the constructive assessment and for highlighting the practical
342	value of the signal-ratio metric. Several of the concerns are addressed in the appendices,
343	which we agree we should have presented more prominently; we clarify each below and will do
344	so in the revision.
345	
346	**W1 (memory of raw routing).** *We understand the worry — "routing on raw inputs" sounds
347	like it should be memory-heavy; in fact it is the opposite.* The router reads a single
348	univariate window and is an **853-parameter** Conv1d gate —
349	**0.002% of the ~40M backbone, 57× smaller than 49K-param DLinear** — adding **<0.1 ms** to
350	the backbone's 52.9 ms forward (**~0.003% of FLOPs**). Total overhead across all three
351	variants is **+5.9% latency (56.0 vs 52.9 ms)** and **+6 MB on a 359 MB backbone (+1.7%)**
352	(Table B.1); memory is set by the frozen backbone every adapter shares.
353	
354	**W2 (dataset-distributional / feature-asymmetry factors).** This is a fair ask. R(D) is in
355	fact designed as a dataset-distributional quantity — computed from raw dataset statistics,
356	predicting per-dataset vulnerability (ρ=−0.88), with Traffic (R=0.14) and Solar (R=0.06) as
357	the boundary/outlier cases — and App. D.1 adds rate-distortion and information-bottleneck
358	framings toward a broader account (what each framing says is spelled out under Point 6). We do agree that feature asymmetries beyond location–scale
359	are not yet formalized, and we see formalizing them as a valuable direction for future theory
360	(see Point 2).
361	
362	**W3 (scaling experts → router-input dimensionality / bandwidth).** This is a natural worry,
363	since in a standard MoE the router input does grow with the expert count. Here it does not:
364	the router input is the raw window and is **independent of K**; only the K-way logit layer (64→K) grows,
365	which is negligible. Because routing is **Top-2, exactly two experts execute per sample
366	regardless of K**, so both active compute *and* memory traffic are **O(2), not O(K)** — bandwidth
367	does not grow with the expert count by construction. Table I.2 (K∈{1..10}) is the empirical
368	performance-stability check (within ±10% for K≥2); larger learned or dynamically-generated
369	pools beyond K=10 are future work. So expert count does not create a router-input or bandwidth
370	bottleneck.
371	
372	**W4 (other normalizers: BatchNorm/LayerNorm/RMSNorm).** App. H directly tests this:
373	swapping RevIN for **BatchNorm1d** and **GroupNorm** yields identical collapse
374	(entropy→0.004 / 0.000 — i.e. one expert, vs the log 5 ≈ 1.61 uniform maximum), while
375	removing normalization keeps it healthy (0.82). `[NEW]` To match this interventional rigor for
376	LayerNorm specifically, we also swap in a **LayerNorm at MOMENT's input-normalization position**
377	(same App H protocol: AdaMix, last-4 unfreeze, ETTh1, seed 42): it **collapses identically
378	(entropy → 0.000)**, with the no-normalization control healthy at 0.825 (reproducing App H's 0.817). The apparent tension
379	with our **LayerNorm/RMSNorm negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL)** is resolved by *where* the
380	norm sits: at the input position LayerNorm strips per-window statistics and collapses, whereas an
381	**encoder-internal** LayerNorm/RMSNorm does not strip the router's input and does not collapse.
382	The rule is *whether the normalizer strips routing-relevant statistics at the router's input*.
383	
384	**W5 (only forecasting/imputation).** See Common Response (point 3): + input-length
385	ablation `[NEW]` and a classification mechanism check `[NEW]`.
386	
387	**W6 / Q3 (few epochs / convergence / 200 epochs).** The complex dual-stream Residual-IA⁺
388	reaches its validation optimum early (logged early-stop 7–20 epochs) and *overfits* by 50;
389	the simpler RR-MoA is robust to longer training (below). Extending the *baseline* full-FT
390	to 50 and 100 epochs (90-config sweep) still loses to 15-epoch frozen RR-MoA by 33–71%
391	(App. O). `[NEW]` We now train RR-MoA to **200 epochs** on ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather **and
392	Electricity** (the dataset flagged as slowest to converge; 3 seeds each): routing **never
393	collapses** (seed-mean entropy 1.02–1.34, minimum 0.87 across all 12 runs, vs a 0.00 collapse
394	floor), with **Electricity the healthiest at 1.34**. MSE is stable-to-improved versus the
395	15-epoch numbers (ETTh1 0.680→0.646, ETTm1 0.564→0.493, Weather 0.276→0.271; Electricity 0.314).
396	Long training therefore neither destabilizes routing nor erodes the advantage: the reported
397	15-epoch MSEs are conservative, not a convergence artifact.
398	
399	**W7 (statistical corrections may be too conservative).** The reviewer is right that an
400	over-conservative correction risks *false negatives*. `[NEW]` We re-analyzed the archived
401	per-run MSEs and address both directions. **(i) Our claimed effect is correction-immaterial.**
402	Re-running the *pooled* Wilcoxon signed-rank on the RR-MoA-vs-best-fixed cells gives
403	**p ≈ 3×10⁻¹¹ uncorrected**, so Bonferroni over every comparison in the paper still leaves it
404	below 10⁻⁹, and the more powerful Holm/BH only lower it further; no correction hides it. (A
405	per-*dataset* Wilcoxon with 3–7 seeds is limited by seed count, not effect size, since an n=3
406	signed-rank floors at p=0.125, which is precisely why the headline significance is the pooled
407	test plus the 54/54 win-count rather than per-dataset p-values.) **(ii) The boundary null is
408	genuine.** On Traffic (R=0.14), RR-MoA does *not* beat the best fixed adapter even under the
409	most powerful *uncorrected* test (+2.9%, **p=0.88**), so the null is a real falsification, not a
410	strict-correction artifact. Solar (R=0.06) is by contrast not a null but the low-R *outlier*
411	where RR-MoA improves (−32.9%, Table `exchange_solar`). We will report these uncorrected and
412	Holm/BH values alongside Bonferroni in the revision.
413	
414	**Q1 (apply raw routing to existing MoE, e.g. AdaMix).** We did exactly this. **AdaMix-Raw**
415	(App., Table `adamix_raw`) swaps only AdaMix's hidden-state router for a raw-input router,
416	leaving its experts and training loop unchanged: routing entropy recovers from near-collapse
417	to near-uniform (0.49→1.55, of a 1.61 maximum) and MSE improves **42–88%** across all 12 cells. This isolates the **router input** as the
418	dominant cause, exactly the clarification requested.
419	
420	**Q2 (generality to image / other domains).** App. H.1 replicates the mechanism in vision:
